title: Homogenization at a polynomial scale in high contrast
authors: Scott Armstrong · Tuomo Kuusi · Amélie Loher

A.title: Polynomial entry into small contrast
A.short: How far must we zoom out?
A.statement: Assume (P1)–(P3). For every σ ∈ (0,1], there is C(σ,d,γ) < ∞ such that Θm ≤ 1 + σ for every m ≥ m_ent := ⌈C log₃(2 + ΠKΨ)⌉.
A.formula: Θm ≤ 1 + σ    for all m ≥ ⌈C log₃(2 + ΠKΨ)⌉
A.meaning: A polynomially bounded observation length is sufficient for the averaged primal and dual descriptions to nearly agree.
A.scope: The scale is sufficient, not necessarily minimal. Small contrast is agreement of primal and dual descriptions, not isotropy.
A.goal: Polynomial entry at every sufficiently large standard scale

steps.title: Plan backward from the gap closure
opens: Find an admissible interval with small histories and an adapted grid
Close the duality gap on standard cubes
Keep the total scale index O(log(2 + ΠKΨ))
steps.observation: The destination is a small primal–dual mismatch. Proposition 5.3 can supply it from a carefully selected interval, provided its tolerances and response time are fixed first.
steps.move: Fix σ ∈ (0,1]. In Proposition 5.3 set δ = σ; choose H, then the determinant tolerance τ. Reduce the theorem to a selected interval, gap closure on standard cubes, and a logarithmic total scale budget.
steps.verification: B-L: instantiate Proposition 5.3 in that parameter order. Choose the parameters of Proposition 2.1 at tolerance τ and B ≥ max{B₀, Bresp}. These constants depend only on σ,d,γ. The new goals are conjunctive, not alternatives.
steps.proof: Fix the target tolerance σ. Choose H and then τ from Proposition 5.3 with δ = σ. Fix L, η, B₀ as in Proposition 2.1 and then B ≥ max{B₀,Bresp}. It remains to produce the selection inputs and bound every scale increment.
steps.detail: This is a strategic choice of a sufficient route. It does not assert that the selected interval already exists. The subsequent toolkit calls inherit the same parameter choices. This is why the constants may depend on σ,d,γ but not on the coefficient law or Π.

alternative.title: Choose all tolerances independently
alternative.reason: The hypotheses of the final comparison require an order of smallness. Arbitrary fixed values need not satisfy those inequalities.
alternative.cost: Missing hypothesis check; no search-cost estimate.

steps.title: Initialize the error histories once
fact: Controlled fluctuation and mean histories after logarithmically many scales
steps.observation: Independent blocks average well, but a larger-block matrix is only bounded by their average. The positive discrepancy is measured by the decrease of the mean.
steps.move: Choose j* to satisfy (5.9), then use the fixed-grid estimates and Proposition 5.1 on the Euclidean grid.
steps.verification: B-L: P2 gives independence for separated blocks; P3 and the tail growth supply the required moments. Subadditivity gives a positive semidefinite discrepancy. Proposition 5.1 controls the retained histories; j* ≤ C log₃(2 + ΠKΨ).
steps.proof: Take j* minimal in (5.9). Its bound is C log₃(2 + ΠKΨ). The Euclidean initialization in Proposition 5.1 uses the fixed-grid estimates to reduce fluctuation and mean-history errors to the prescribed tolerance with logarithmic scale cost.
steps.detail: The average of independent block matrices is not equal to the larger-block matrix. Their difference has a sign, and its expected value is the mean decrease. The logarithmic determinant loss controls this drift and the changing normalization. This initialization supplies estimates, not a small duality gap.

alternative.title: Identify a coarse matrix with a block average
alternative.reason: Subadditivity gives an inequality, not an equality. Discarding the positive discrepancy drops the mean-drift contribution.
alternative.cost: The claimed recurrence would be unjustified.

steps.title: Carry the estimates across changing grids
fact: Nearby-grid comparisons preserve enough history to continue
steps.observation: Anisotropy makes Euclidean geometry expensive. A better grid changes with the mean matrix, so its estimates must survive a change of shape.
steps.move: Use gradual geometry updates and the retained histories, with the comparisons of §4, rather than restarting the preparation on every grid.
steps.verification: B-L: apply the nearby-grid comparisons under their small incoming-error and drift conditions. Boundary pieces have summable contributions because γ < 1. Startup restores the fixed-grid recurrence; the update itself need not reduce error.
steps.proof: Transport the fluctuation and mean histories to nearby adapted grids using §4. Large old-grid cubes fill most of a new cube; smaller boundary cubes are controlled using P3. The condition γ < 1 makes the fine-scale contribution summable.
steps.detail: The relevant comparison is geometric: a boundary volume factor offsets the coarse-ellipticity loss. Schematically the small-scale sum has factors 3^{(1−γ)r}, r < 0. Its convergence explains the strict restriction γ < 1. The proof keeps the earlier estimates because a new boundary intersects many scales.

alternative.title: Restart preparation after every improvement
alternative.reason: The paper explains that the earlier [AK25] organization repeats a logarithmic preparation over logarithmically many stages. That yields a squared-log scale bound instead of the desired logarithmic one.
alternative.cost: O(log² contrast) scale indices in the earlier argument; this is a weaker proven bound, not an impossibility result.

steps.title: Count geometry and errors in one budget
fact: An admissible interval [s,t], t = s + H, within the joint scale budget
steps.observation: Errors can increase when the grid improves. Counting only error decreases would miss those costs; counting both types of progress can pay for them together.
steps.move: Apply the scale-selection mechanism through Proposition 5.2, combining logarithmic error, shape mismatch, and determinant losses.
steps.verification: B-L: initialization supplies the starting histories; §4 supplies the update and startup bounds; Proposition 2.1 supplies the joint count. Proposition 5.2 returns (5.11)–(5.13) and t ≤ j* + ⌈(B + C(H,τ,d,γ)) log₃(2 + Π)⌉.
steps.proof: Proposition 5.2 supplies an interval [s,t] with t = s + H, small retained histories, small mean variation, and suitable adapted geometry. The terminal scale satisfies t ≤ j* + ⌈(B + C(H,τ,d,γ)) log₃(2 + Π)⌉.
steps.detail: This is the main organizational gain of the paper. Fixed-grid contraction, partial geometry improvements, and determinant losses are charged to one count. Failed determinant tests and temporary error increases remain in that count. The selected interval is forced by a bounded progress budget; the argument is not a numerical search for a lucky cube.

alternative.title: Use only a fluctuation-decrease counter
alternative.reason: A geometry update may enlarge the error. A counter that ignores geometry and determinant jumps does not control the total number of updates.
alternative.cost: No logarithmic total-budget proof follows from this reduced counter.

steps.title: Turn the selected estimates into gap closure
fact: The primal–dual gap is small on the selected adapted cube
steps.observation: Small fluctuations say the random matrix is concentrated around its mean. They do not say that its mean agrees with the dual. Optimizer energies connect these two questions.
steps.move: Use the primal and dual optimizer comparison in Steps 3–6 of Proposition 5.3, with terminal loads and the selected fixed grid.
steps.verification: B-L: the selected histories and determinant control provide the small error terms required by Proposition 5.3. Its centered-energy estimates and absorption establish (5.34) on the adapted cube. The load normalization and grid hypotheses are essential toolkit premises.
steps.proof: Apply the optimizer comparison of Proposition 5.3 to the selected interval. Bounds on centered gradients and fluxes, together with the equation and small histories, control the centered energies and close the duality gap on the adapted cube.
steps.detail: One cannot replace this with “the variance is small, therefore homogenization holds.” Concentration alone does not identify the relation between two mean variational quantities. This is an imported, substantial analytic argument: this explorer exposes its role and inputs, while pp.60–65 contain its full energy estimates.

alternative.title: Infer a small gap from small variance alone
alternative.reason: A random quantity can be almost deterministic while two different mean quantities remain separated. Fluctuation control alone does not compare primal and dual energies.
alternative.cost: Missing implication, not an infinite search lower bound.

steps.title: Return to Euclidean cubes
fact: Θ at a Euclidean entry scale is at most 1 + σ
steps.observation: The good estimate lives on an adapted cube; the theorem is stated on standard cubes. Geometry and matrix order must both survive the transfer.
steps.move: Complete Proposition 5.3 with the two opposite Whitney comparisons in Step 7.
steps.verification: B-L: the adapted gap and polynomial eccentricity control imply a standard-cube bound at most C(σ,d,γ) log₃(2 + Π) additional scales later. The tolerance choices in (5.31) make the final error at most σ.
steps.proof: The final part of Proposition 5.3 gives a Euclidean scale m_entry > t with Θ at that scale ≤ 1 + σ and m_entry − t ≤ C(σ,d,γ) log₃(2 + Π). Opposite comparisons control the primal and dual sides.
steps.detail: A bound in convenient coordinates is not yet the displayed theorem. The transfer cost is logarithmic because the eccentricity is bounded polynomially in the reference contrast. All geometry costs must be included before claiming a polynomial physical length.

alternative.title: Simply rename the adapted cube a standard cube
alternative.reason: The domains and normalized energy comparisons differ. Relabeling does not transport a bound between them.
alternative.cost: Requires a geometric comparison and its scale cost.

steps.title: Add the costs; close the theorem
fact: For all m ≥ ⌈C log₃(2 + ΠKΨ)⌉, Θm ≤ 1 + σ
steps.observation: All three scale expenses are logarithmic. Adding them preserves that order, whereas restarting preparation could multiply costs.
steps.move: Add initialization, selection, and transfer costs, enlarge C, and use persistence of the primal–dual contrast bound at larger standard scales.
steps.verification: B-C: sum the three upper bounds and absorb constants depending only on σ,d,γ. B-L: the ordered primal and dual matrices preserve the small-contrast bound at larger scales. B-C: 3^{⌈Cx⌉} ≤ 3·3^{Cx}, so the physical length is polynomial.
steps.proof: Adding the bounds gives a sufficient deterministic entry index m_ent = ⌈C(σ,d,γ) log₃(2 + ΠKΨ)⌉. The small-contrast bound holds at every larger standard scale. Thus 3^{m_ent} ≤ 3(2 + ΠKΨ)^{C(σ,d,γ)}, as claimed.
steps.detail: The meeting is now exact: the established fact includes the tolerance, all larger scales, and the required dependence of the constant. The theorem gives a sufficient entry scale, not the earliest possible one. No estimate uniform as γ approaches 1 is asserted.

alternative.title: State the bound directly in physical length
alternative.reason: Exponentiating the scale-index bound gives the stated polynomial length bound; rounding contributes the factor 3. This is a rephrasing of the same completed argument.
alternative.cost: No additional analytic cost; no independent alternative proof.

B.title: Algebraic convergence at a polynomial scale
B.statement: Assume (P1)–(P3). There exist C(d,γ) < ∞, κ(d,γ) > 0 and a deterministic m₀ ≤ ⌈C log₃(2 + ΠKΨ)⌉ such that Θm₀₊ⱼ − 1 ≤ 3^{−κj} for j ∈ ℕ. There is a deterministic symmetric positive definite 2d × 2d matrix A∞ with 0 ≤ A(□m₀₊ⱼ) − A∞ ≤ 6·3^{−κj}A∞. Its blocks satisfy s* = s > 0 and k = −kᵀ; the effective coefficient is ā = s + k.
B.meaning: Once the starting scale is reached, the mismatch decays algebraically with length and the coarse matrices approach an effective limit.
B.scope: Contrast affects the starting scale; κ depends only on d,γ. These are annealed matrix estimates, not yet realization-by-realization PDE error estimates.
B.goal: An algebraic rate and an identified positive definite effective limit

steps.title: Enter the small-error regime
fact: After dilation, the scale-zero annealed contrast is at most 1 + σ
opens: Obtain Θm₀₊ⱼ − 1 ≤ 3^{−κj} with m₀ = O(log(2 + ΠKΨ))
Identify a positive definite effective matrix and its Loewner error bound
steps.observation: The nonlinear iteration only contracts when the mismatch is already small. Theorem A supplies this starting point at a polynomial length.
steps.move: Choose σ = σ(d,γ) small enough for the later absorption; apply Theorem A and dilate by 3^{m_ent}. Reduce the conclusion to a decay rate and a compatible positive definite limit.
steps.verification: B-L: P1–P3 are the hypotheses of Theorem A. Integer triadic dilation preserves stationarity and gives dependence range ≤ 1. The new random scale is 3^{−m_ent}S; increasing Ψ makes the old tail bound admissible. Both remaining goals are required.
steps.proof: Apply Theorem A at a sufficiently small tolerance σ(d,γ). For the dilated law a(3^{m_ent}·), scale zero has contrast at most 1 + σ. The assumptions remain valid, with the same reference block and an admissible original tail function.
steps.detail: The dilation changes the unit of length, not the theorem’s assumptions. P[3^{−m_ent}S > t] ≤ Ψ(3^{m_ent}t)⁻¹ ≤ Ψ(t)⁻¹. At the end the scale shift must be restored. Smallness here concerns the annealed mismatch, not the original microscopic contrast.

alternative.title: Run the nonlinear iteration from the microscopic scale
alternative.reason: The quadratic terms are not absorbable from an arbitrarily large mismatch using this argument. The required smallness premise is absent.
alternative.cost: This iteration has no justified contraction before entry.

steps.title: Normalize and initialize bounded moments
fact: Uniform normalized moments after a logarithmic startup b
steps.observation: Small annealed contrast does not bound every random block. The variance estimates need high moments controlled independently of the original contrast.
steps.move: Use the Schur complement of F = A(□₀) to choose an adapted grid. Start from a polynomial bound H and increase b by O(log(H/σ)).
steps.verification: B-L: P3 and the moments of S yield (6.1). Independent coloring and boundary filling give (6.2)–(6.4). The boundary sum converges since γ < 1. B-C: choosing b logarithmically makes H3^{−b} small and gives uniform normalized L^Q bounds and comparable means.
steps.proof: Step 1 of §6.1 chooses a Schur-complement adapted grid and H ≤ C(2 + ΠKΨ)^C. Fine-scale moments, finite-range averaging, and boundary estimates give a startup b ≤ C log₃(H/σ) beyond which the normalized moments and mean comparisons are uniform.
steps.detail: The boundary estimate contains H Σ_{r<0}3^{r−j}3^{−γr}, bounded by CH3^{−j}. This is where γ < 1 enters again. Delaying the start absorbs the polynomial factor H into a logarithmic number of scales rather than carrying it into the decay exponent.

alternative.title: Use annealed smallness as a high-moment bound
alternative.reason: Control of an expectation does not by itself control the L^Q size of random blocks. The fluctuation estimate requires those moments.
alternative.cost: The missing startup must still be paid for.

steps.title: Couple fluctuations to an earlier mismatch
fact: vₖ ≤ C aℓ² + C3^{−d(k−ℓ)} for b ≤ ℓ ≤ k
steps.observation: Averaging many separated blocks improves variance, but the remaining mean mismatch contributes an error. Its square becomes useful once the mismatch is small.
steps.move: Introduce the nonnegative decreasing mismatch aⱼ and the normalized variance vⱼ; apply the finite-range averaging estimate.
steps.verification: B-L: the uniform moments, adapted-grid separation, and small-contrast normalization are the premises used in (6.6), via Lemma 3.2 and [AK25, Lemma 4.4]. The mismatch satisfies 0 ≤ aⱼ ≤ Cσ.
steps.proof: Let aⱼ = d⁻¹ tr(S*ⱼ⁻¹ Sⱼ) − 1 and let vⱼ be the normalized matrix variance from §6.1. The sequence aⱼ is nonnegative and decreasing. Equation (6.6) yields vₖ ≤ C aℓ² + C3^{−d(k−ℓ)} for b ≤ ℓ ≤ k.
steps.detail: This is a two-quantity argument. Variance is reduced by averaging, while the squared mismatch is a nonlinear remainder. Simply iterating variance would not yet yield a recurrence for aⱼ. The next comparison supplies that missing direction.

alternative.title: Track variance without the mismatch
alternative.reason: A small variance does not identify the primal–dual gap. The coupled term and the optimizer comparison cannot be discarded.
alternative.cost: The target quantity is no longer controlled.

steps.title: Convert optimizer control into a recurrence
fact: aₙ is bounded by weighted variances, mean decreases, and a decaying tail
steps.observation: To improve the mismatch, compare optimizer energies. Their weak-norm estimates see both fluctuations and the decrease of the mean across scales.
steps.move: Control the positive-excess maximum Mₙ, apply the weak-norm optimizer comparison, and absorb Caₙ² using the small entry tolerance.
steps.verification: B-L: choose ρ = (1+γ)/2 and Q as in the paper so ζ = ρ−d/Q > γ; (6.5) bounds Mₙ. With β = (1−ρ)/2 > 0, the comparison gives (6.7) for n ≥ b+4. Increase b so the prefactor is controlled. The cited analytic estimates are toolkit dependencies.
steps.proof: The maximum estimate (6.5) controls coarse-ellipticity excess. The optimizer comparison, including [AK25, Lemma 2.16], yields aₙ ≤ C Σ_{k=b}^n 3^{−β(n−k)}(vₖ + aₖ − aₙ) + C3^{−β(n−b)}, after absorbing the quadratic term.
steps.detail: The expression aₖ − aₙ is a nonnegative mean decrease for k ≤ n. Keeping the negative copies of aₙ matters: they later strengthen the coefficient on the left. This is a sourced summary of the estimates on pp.68–69, not an elementary derivation of the imported weak-norm lemma.

alternative.title: Drop the negative copies of aₙ
alternative.reason: The resulting weaker inequality loses the explicit strict-contraction mechanism used on p.70. The remaining coefficients need not sum to less than one.
alternative.cost: A different argument would be needed to recover a rate.

steps.title: Absorb the delayed square and contract
fact: aₙ ≤ C3^{−c(n−b)} on the adapted grid
steps.observation: The weighted negative mismatch terms create a strict contraction margin. Smallness can pay for the delayed quadratic terms inside that margin.
steps.move: Set uⱼ = a_{b+j}, use ℓ = b + ⌈3i/4⌉ in the variance bound, and prove uⱼ ≤ Mrʲ by induction for a suitable r < 1.
steps.verification: B-C: substitute (6.6) into (6.7) to get (6.8); move the negative uⱼ terms left. B-L: choose r near 1 so the linear weighted operator is a strict contraction. For i > 3 the delayed index is earlier; bound its square by (Cσ)^{2/3}M^{4/3}rⁱ. Handle i ≤ 3 by (Cσ)², choose M, then σ small.
steps.proof: Equation (6.8) couples uⱼ to weighted uᵢ − uⱼ and u²_{⌈3i/4⌉}. Moving the negative terms to the left produces a strict contraction. Induction and the uniform bound uᵢ ≤ Cσ absorb the delayed square. Consequently aₙ ≤ C3^{−c(n−b)}.
steps.detail: Let q₀ = 3^{−β} and Tⱼ = Σ_{h=1}^j q₀ʰ. The left coefficient becomes 1 + ATⱼ. At r = 1 the corresponding linear ratio is at most AT∞/(1 + AT∞) < 1, so a nearby r < 1 still works. The few indices where the delay is not strictly earlier must be handled separately; ignoring them would make an induction circular.

alternative.title: Use monotonicity alone to infer a geometric rate
alternative.reason: A positive decreasing sequence may decay arbitrarily slowly. For example 1/(j+1) is decreasing but is not bounded by Mrʲ for any fixed M and 0 < r < 1.
alternative.cost: Qualitative convergence alone does not supply the claimed rate.
source: Rate mechanism in §6.1 Step 3; sequence counterexample is explanatory

steps.title: Transfer the rate and restore physical scales
steps.observation: The adapted-grid rate still carries a geometry error when returned to standard cubes. A further logarithmic shift absorbs its polynomial prefactor.
steps.move: Apply the adapted-to-standard comparison, choose n = ⌊m/2⌋ + b, absorb H, and restore the initial dilation.
steps.verification: B-L: [AK25, Lemma 2.15] and E₀ ≤ HF give Θm − 1 ≤ Caₙ + CH3^{−(m−n)}. B-C: the stated choice balances decaying terms for m ≥ 2b+2. Add C log₃ H scales to absorb prefactors, reduce the exponent if needed, and add m_ent.
steps.proof: The comparison gives Θm − 1 ≤ Caₙ + CH3^{−(m−n)} for m > n ≥ b. Set n = ⌊m/2⌋ + b. A shift of C log₃ H absorbs the prefactor. Restoring the original length unit yields (1.10)–(1.11), with κ depending only on d,γ.
steps.detail: Contrast affects when the decay begins; it does not enter κ. Geometric decay in the index j is algebraic decay in the length ratio R/R₀ = 3ʲ, since 3^{−κj} = (R/R₀)^{−κ}. The paper does not specify numerical constants for a calibrated prediction.

alternative.title: Rewrite decay in terms of length ratio
alternative.reason: The identity R/R₀ = 3ʲ turns 3^{−κj} into (R/R₀)^{−κ}. This explains the word algebraic; it does not change the proof.
alternative.cost: Exact reparameterization, no new search cost.

steps.title: Identify the effective matrix and close
fact: A∞ is positive definite and 0 ≤ A(□m₀₊ⱼ) − A∞ ≤ 6·3^{−κj}A∞
steps.observation: Monotone matrices have a limit if bounded, but a uniform positive lower bound is needed to keep it invertible. Vanishing primal–dual mismatch then identifies its block structure.
steps.move: Use the primal–dual sandwich, pass to the limit in the dual comparison, and use order reversal under inversion to estimate the error.
steps.verification: B-L: subadditivity and dual order bound all matrices between fixed positive definite matrices, so the decreasing limit is positive definite. Equation (4.7) and the vanishing gap imply self-duality. Comparing blocks gives s* = s > 0 and k = −kᵀ. The same order estimate gives (1.12).
steps.proof: The standard-cube means decrease between fixed positive definite bounds, hence converge to A∞ > 0. The primal–dual comparison and Θm → 1 make A∞ self-dual. Its blocks satisfy s* = s and k = −kᵀ, defining the effective coefficient ā = s + k. Finally 0 ≤ A(□m) − A∞ ≤ 6(Θm − 1)A∞; insert the established rate.
steps.detail: Matrix inequalities are in Loewner order: their difference is positive semidefinite. The 2d × 2d variational matrix A∞ is distinct from the d × d effective coefficient ā. Theorem B is an annealed result. Bounds on a particular realization’s PDE solutions require Theorems C or D and additional arguments.

alternative.title: Infer invertibility from monotonicity alone
alternative.reason: Positive definite matrices can decrease to a singular limit: j⁻¹I tends to zero. The fixed positive lower bound is essential to this passage.
alternative.cost: Missing nondegeneracy premise, not proof of universal irreplacability.
